112.0.s.en: (1) The attributes of him who fears the Lord

112.0.0.en: "Praise ye the LORD. Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD, that delighteth greatly in his commandments."

112.0.1.en: 1- The psalm begins with rejoicing, that is, the praise of God, and at the outset it blesses him who fears the Lord, who, as we learned at the end of the previous psalm, is the wise man, and who is therefore able to praise God continually, to rejoice before Him, and to walk in His commandments.

112.0.2.en: 2- The demons fear God, and so do the wicked, but they do not love His commandments or walk in them; therefore he continues his words in this verse, saying that the true fearer of the Lord is the one who delights in His commandments, who loves them and desires them with all his heart, and is indeed greatly delighted in them. Thus the love of God and the fear of Him are mingled, and are united in a wonderful way that only he knows who has experienced it through keeping God's commandments.

112.1.0.en: "His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed."

112.1.1.en: 1- God blesses not only those who fear Him but also their offspring on earth, in addition to the blessings of heaven that He gives them. The might of the offspring does not mean the multitude of their number or their bodily or material strength, but rather their spiritual strength, so that they too live in the fear of God and enjoy His blessings in their lives.

112.1.2.en: 2- God's goods are many, and He gives them to His upright children, that is, those who fear Him and keep His commandments, and they are the blessed offspring, and not only the bodily children of those who fear the Lord but also the spiritual children. The patriarchs, bishops, monks and celibates, whether in the Old Testament, such as Elijah and Jeremiah, or in the New Testament, such as Paul, had many spiritual children, far more than any bodily children of any pious men.

112.2.0.en: "Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever." Wealth: ample provision and great riches.

112.2.1.en: 1- God blesses those who fear Him and gives them not only their material needs but gives them abundance and ease in material things, so that they are not preoccupied with them and their only concern is life with Him. And to the extent that they are occupied with God, He grants them material things, and they distribute these to the needy, as the believers used to lay their gifts at the feet of the Apostles, so that the Apostles were in plenty, to satisfy the Church with their spiritual teachings and also their material needs.

112.2.2.en: 2- One of the most important attributes of him who fears the Lord is that he is righteous, that is, he lives with God and loves Him and walks in His commandments, loves the virtues and longs for the heavens, so that he lives spiritually until he enters the Kingdom. The righteous one here is not only the one who is righteous on earth, but rather it means Christ, the Righteous and Holy One.

112.2.3.en: 3- By this we see that the righteous man enjoys material wealth in his house, that is, he is settled in this wealth, in addition to his enjoyment of righteousness, that is, the spiritual life; so he receives a material portion on earth in addition to a righteousness that endures forever in heaven.

112.3.0.en: "Unto the upright there ariseth light in the darkness: he is gracious, and full of compassion, and righteous."

112.3.1.en: 1- He speaks here of God, who has made His light arise upon His righteous children, upright in their spiritual walk, who were in the darkness of affliction, so that their hearts were comforted, as He did with the three youths in the furnace and Daniel in the lions' den. And this light illumined the souls of His righteous children, so that they too became light to those around them through their righteous lives which they received from Him, just as the moon draws its light from the sun.

112.3.2.en: 2- God is also gracious and full of compassion, so He has pity on His children in their afflictions, and if they sin He accepts their repentance, but at the same time He is righteous, that is, just, so He rewards them for all their labors, and disciplines them if they turn away from Him, as He disciplined His people with the captivity. And the righteous children of God learned these attributes from Him, so their hearts were filled with graciousness and compassion toward all those around them, but at the same time their justice and firmness appear toward the careless and the licentious, so they discipline them that they may repent, as Paul excommunicated the sinner of the city of Corinth.

112.3.3.en: Remember God, and set Him before you at all times by repeating His holy name, so that you protect yourself by the fear of Him and reject evil however small, and hasten to Him with repentance if you sin, so that your heart is purified and His secrets are disclosed to you, and you cling to Him and He pours out His mercies upon you, and you praise Him with joy.

112.4.0.en: "A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion."

112.4.2.en: 1- The righteous man imitates God, so he becomes merciful, has compassion and pity on the poor and lends to them, so he gladdens their hearts and in turn becomes happy himself. He is compassionate: he gives the poor gifts, and also gives them loans, and helps them in every way so that they may be able to continue their lives.

112.4.3.en: 2- This righteous man orders his affairs with justice; that is, without malice or evil purpose, because his heart is pure, and at the same time his management is just, that is, balanced, so that he does not go to excess in his loans to others to the point that he himself is in need and enters into hardships (2 Cor 8:14), nor does he reduce his help to the poor very much, so that he becomes hard. And this merciful righteous man, because he helped the poor on earth, will have rest and happiness in heaven; because "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again" (Prov 19:17), so God rewards him in heaven.

112.5.0.en: "Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance."

112.5.1.en: 1- He who fears the Lord, the righteous man, is not moved from his principles, but remains holding fast to his righteousness and to the fear of God, for he is a man of principles and values. Nor is he moved from the work of mercy and compassion toward the needy. So he is established in God, and God establishes him with Himself forever.

112.5.2.en: 2- This righteous man or just man is remembered after his death, indeed forever, where he is rewarded in eternity. And just as the works of God are remembered forever (Ps 111:4), so also His righteous children's works, which they did by the power of God, are remembered forever, and they are works of righteousness and mercy.

112.6.0.en: 7- He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD.

112.6.1.en: "See his desire upon his enemies": he sees the punishment of those who trouble him.

112.6.2.en: 1- He who fears the Lord is not afraid of the evil tidings that Satan stirs up against him, but his heart remains steadfast in faith, because he trusts in God, and God gives him this steadfastness which surpasses the mind; for the mind alone is troubled, but faith surpasses it and gives steadiness to man's feelings, so that he goes on living and walking in tranquility and does all his works successfully. The righteous man is liable to hear or to meet with evil tidings, and God permits this to test his faith and steadfastness and spiritual growth.

112.6.3.en: 2- The heart of him who fears the Lord and is merciful to the poor remains steadfast throughout his life, until at the end, that is, in eternity, he sees the punishment of the demons who troubled him in eternal torment, in addition to his victory over the demons who troubled him in life, in his repentance, his striving and his service, and his ability to do mercy to the needy.

112.7.0.en: "He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honour." His horn shall be exalted: the horn is the strongest part of an animal's body, and its being exalted, that is, standing in defiance in readiness to attack the prey, means a declaration of its strength. What is meant is that God declares the strength and glory of the righteous man before all.

112.7.1.en: 1- He who fears the Lord is distinguished by giving and by compassion toward the poor, and by this he brings about justice in the equality of all, when the poor man receives his right and lives, for this is his right, like the right of the rich man to life.

112.7.2.en: 2- God rewards the merciful righteous man, giving him strength and glory by the exalting of his horn in this life in part, that is, in some situations, and gives him victory over Satan, and then in the eternal life he will have true glory. For he who honors the brethren of the Lord will surely be honored by the Lord and rewarded in heaven.

112.8.0.en: "The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish."

112.8.1.en: "Gnash with his teeth": he grinds and presses his teeth together as an expression of his intense rage.

112.8.2.en: 1- The wicked man cannot bear to see virtue and the doing of good; the wicked man is Satan, or every man who walks in evil, who is enraged when he sees good and is troubled within, and his conscience pricks him, and he is in sorrow. The writer of the psalm expresses the wretched state of the wicked man, not in gloating over him, but in grief for him and an attempt to warn him, that he may repent and be saved from this severe distress.

112.8.3.en: 2- All the evil desires in the heart of the wicked man are in vain, for they pass away, that is, they do not benefit him in life, and in addition they end in eternity, and after them come the gnashing of teeth and rage in eternal torment. All this is because the knowledge of God and fellowship with Him do not exist among the wicked, neither on earth nor in the other life.

112.8.4.en: If mercy gives all these blessings, hasten to it; that is, seek out every needy person, whether materially, psychologically or spiritually, and offer him your love in any form, for it is very precious to God, and it gladdens Him, and gladdens you also.

112.8.5.en: Praise of the God of the humble "Alleluia. Praise, O ye servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD" (v. 1) Introduction:

112.8.6.en: 1- Its author: the psalm has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms and its author is unknown, although some attribute it to David.

112.8.7.en: 2- When was it written: if David is its author, it was probably written toward the end of his life, after he had sat on the throne of the kingdom of Israel.

112.8.8.en: 3- This psalm is one of the Hallel psalms, and we have already said that Psalms 111-113 magnify God, of whom it was said in Psalm 110 that He ascended into heaven, and all of them begin with the word Alleluia.

112.8.9.en: 4- Psalms 113 and 114 were said before eating the Passover "and then Psalms 115-118 were said after eating the Passover.

112.8.10.en: 5- This psalm is a liturgical psalm, that is, it is sung in communal worship at the three great feasts, which are the Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, in addition to the feast of the Dedication mentioned in the books of the Maccabees (1 Macc 4:36-49; 2 Macc 10:1-8).

112.8.11.en: 6- This psalm resembles the prayer of Hannah, the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 2:2), and the canticle of the Virgin (Lk 1:47-55).

112.8.12.en: 7- In the Book of Psalms there is a group of psalms called the Hallel psalms, and they are three groups:

112.8.14.en: b - The Great Hallel psalms (Ps 120-136), which include the psalms of ascents.

112.8.16.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Prime and the prayer of the Ninth Hour, because it contains praise and glorification of God, with which we begin our day, and we also glorify Him at the Ninth Hour because He accomplished our redemption on the cross. And God in His humility cares for the humble, and this encourages everyone who begins his day with the remembrance of God, and shows His humility on the cross at the Ninth Hour.

113.0.0.en: 1- Alleluia. Praise, O ye servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD.

113.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm calls all the servants of the Lord to praise Him. The servants of the Lord are those who have been freed from material things and have become servants of the Lord, because servitude to God is freedom from the material things of the world, and so man is able to be released and praise God, not only with the tongue but with thought and feelings and his whole being and with works also.

113.0.2.en: 2- The praise is for the name of the Lord, and the name of the Lord means His person, and this means the attachment of the hearts of those who praise God to Him, so that they repeat His name, remember Him always and glorify Him. This praise and glorification begins now and continues throughout life, and even extends forever in the Kingdom.

113.1.0.en: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD's name is to be praised."

113.1.1.en: 1- The name of the Lord is praised from the rising of the sun to its going down, that is, throughout the day, and by the day is meant the whole of life. Continual praise is a natural, or spontaneous, duty of the children of God.

113.1.2.en: 2- By the rising of the sun to its going down is meant the Jews who are in the east and the Gentiles who are in the west; all of them praise Him. This verse is a prophecy of the Church of the New Testament, where the Jews and the Gentiles in the whole world believe in Christ and establish churches in every place, in which they raise praises to God at all times, for worship is no longer confined to one place as it was among the Jews.

113.1.3.en: If the praise of God is constant in the heavens, then we should strive on earth to praise God, so that we know Him and enjoy fellowship with Him and love Him, and our heart grows more inflamed and our praise increases.

113.1.4.en: (2) The greatness of God who lifts up the humble (vv. 4-9:)

113.2.0.en: 4- The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens. 5- Who is like unto the LORD our God, who dwelleth on high,

113.2.1.en: 1- The greatness of the Lord rises above all men, because He is their Creator, and His mercies overflow upon all, and He deserves continual praise. And if the Lord is above all nations, and they believed in Him, they will feel that He is their God and will praise Him; how much more should the Jews, who knew God before the Gentiles, praise Him and glorify Him, because He humbled Himself, became incarnate and redeemed them on the cross.

113.2.2.en: 2- The loftiness of God and His greatness are above the heavens, because He is the Creator of all the angels, and there is none like Him in greatness, and the mind of man cannot comprehend the extent of His greatness, nor can even the angels comprehend God. Therefore all His works deserve praise. And this praise benefits those who praise; as for God, He is perfect, but He rejoices in the praise of His children and blesses them.

113.3.0.en: "Who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth!" The things that are humble: the lowly.

113.3.1.en: God, the All-Great, is loving and very humble, indeed He loves the humble and looks upon them with care and tends them, whether in the heavens, that is, the angels, or on the earth, that is, men. Christ showed His humility by His Incarnation, and asked us to learn humility from Him (Mt 11:29) so that we may have compassion on all around us.

113.4.0.en: 7- He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill; 8- That he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people. Princes: great men and rulers.

113.4.1.en: 1- The poor is man, who by his sin went down to the dust after he was driven out of Paradise.

113.4.2.en: And man is also the needy one who dwelt in the dunghill, which is the dunghill of his sins. And Christ became incarnate to live among sinful men, and to receive them to Himself, and to show His love for them in His teachings, the healing of their diseases, the feeding of them, and then in their redemption on the cross.

113.4.3.en: 2- The aim of the Incarnation and redemption is to raise man from the dust and the dunghill, to be exalted to an honorable place that befits him, that is, to become a son of God. For Christ, by His death and resurrection, has become the firstborn among many brethren, that we may rise in Him from our sins and enjoy the honor of sonship to God. And this has happened in the lives of many, such as David the shepherd of sheep who became a king, and the fishermen who became apostles and preached to the world.

113.5.0.en: "He maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children. Praise ye the LORD."

113.5.1.en: The barren woman is the Church of the Gentiles, far from God, and when she believed she had many children who believe in Christ. This verse was fulfilled in many women who were barren, such as Sarah the mother of Isaac, and Rebekah who bore Esau and Jacob, and Hannah the mother of Samuel, and Elizabeth who bore John the Baptist.

113.5.2.en: The humility of God is wonderful, who makes me, the lowly, a son to Him, and raises me from the dust and the dunghill, that I may share with the saints in the enjoyment of fellowship with Him. This impels me to greater humility at His feet, and at the feet of all His children, that I may serve them all the days of my life.

113.5.3.en: God the Almighty Savior "When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language" (v. 1) Introduction:

113.5.4.en: 1- Its author: unknown, because it has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms.

113.5.6.en: This psalm tells us of the crossing of the Red Sea and then of the river Jordan, and therefore the time of its writing is one of these possibilities:

113.5.7.en: a - At the entry into the land of Canaan, at Gilgal, immediately after crossing the river Jordan.

113.5.8.en: b - After David's victories over the nations, in glorification of the mighty God.

113.5.9.en: c - After the return from the captivity, in glorification of God who brought back His people, and as an encouragement to the people to build the temple in Jerusalem.

113.5.10.en: 3- Since the psalm tells us of the crossing of the Red Sea and the Jordan, it encourages the soul that repeats it to come out from under the authority of the devil and his sins, to repentance and the beginning of a new life with God.

113.5.11.en: 4- This psalm is liturgical and was prayed before eating the Passover, which is the most important of the feasts of the children of Israel.

113.5.12.en: 5- This psalm is mentioned in the Laqqan (the washing of the feet) of the feast of Epiphany; it is read before the Gospel, and its mention is repeated during the Liturgy of the Laqqan, to declare the authority of God over the waters. And although Christ was immersed in the waters to fulfill all righteousness for us, He is the Creator of the waters, and all nature is subject to Him.

113.5.13.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
